title: Writing testable acceptance criteria
content: Acceptance criteria should be specific, observable, and testable. Prefer Given/When/Then or clear bullet outcomes that a reviewer can verify without guessing intent. Avoid vague words like "fast" or "user-friendly" unless you define measurable thresholds. Each criterion should map to at least one verification idea, and edge cases should be called out explicitly when they change expected behavior.

title: Splitting oversized stories
content: A story is oversized when it mixes multiple user goals, spans unrelated components, or cannot be demonstrated in one short feedback loop. Split by independent value slices: separate happy path from edge handling, isolate setup work, or cut by persona or workflow step. After a split, each story should still deliver a coherent outcome with its own acceptance criteria and a clear done definition.

title: Exploratory testing charters for story analysis
content: Use a short charter before exploring a story: target (feature or risk), resources (build, data, tools), and a time box. Focus the session on one mission such as "find gaps between written acceptance criteria and actual behavior" or "probe permission boundaries around this workflow." Capture notes as questions, bugs, and follow-up ideas so findings feed story refinement, not only defect tickets.

title: Severity versus priority in QA triage
content: Severity describes impact on users or the system if the defect is true: data loss and security issues are higher severity than cosmetic copy issues. Priority describes when to fix relative to release goals and workarounds. A medium-severity defect can be high priority before a launch; a high-severity defect with a safe workaround may wait. Record both fields separately so triage debates stay precise.

title: Mapping story components to test focus
content: Identify which components a story touches—UI, API, auth, data storage, notifications—and let that drive test focus. Auth changes need session and permission checks; API changes need contract and error-path coverage; UI changes need accessibility and state transitions. When a story spans components, list the highest-risk boundary first and verify integration assumptions before deep happy-path polish.

title: Defect report quality checklist
content: A useful defect report states the expected result, the actual result, and the steps to reproduce with environment details. Include identifiers such as story or build when known, and attach evidence (screenshot, log excerpt, request id) when it shortens diagnosis. Avoid mixing multiple unrelated failures in one report; split them so severity and ownership stay clear.

title: Ambiguity and missing-requirement signals
content: Flag stories that use undefined actors, unspecified error handling, or success criteria that cannot be observed. Watch for missing states such as empty lists, partial failures, retries, and permission denials. When two readers would implement different behavior from the same text, treat that as a requirement gap and ask for an explicit decision before coding or deep test design.

title: Non-functional considerations on stories
content: Even feature stories often imply non-functional expectations: latency, accessibility, security, auditability, or resilience. Ask whether limits, timeouts, or compliance constraints belong in acceptance criteria. If NFRs are deferred, record that choice so QA does not silently assume production-grade behavior that the story never promised.
